finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of calling require_edit(), so the authorization check is never enforced. Any caller can overwrite any document's body (broken access control / IDOR).
finding.source: Any authenticated request user (g.user) sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with a JSON body, where doc_id is attacker-chosen and the user is neither owner nor editor.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, which modifies a protected document.

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> takes an attacker-controlled doc_id.
DOCS[doc_id] is looked up with no ownership scoping. A missing id raises KeyError, giving a 500 and leaking which ids exist.
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns a bool that is ignored, so no abort(403) happens.

finding.guards_checked: require_edit is used correctly in update_title at line 27 but not here. No before_request authentication hook is visible in this file, so g.user is never set or verified here; g.user may be unset, which would raise AttributeError, or it may be set by external code not in this repo. No other decorators or middleware guard the route. can_edit itself is correct but is not enforced.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit (docs.py:7) returns a bool and is called as a bare statement at docs.py:19. require_edit (docs.py:11-13), which aborts with 403, is only used in update_title at line 27. There is no decorator or before_request hook in the repo.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit() and discards the bool, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any user who reaches the route; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is the check that would abort, and it is only used at docs.py:27. Minor point: the claim that g.user is "authenticated" is an assumption, since nothing in the repo sets g.user. That doesn't change the verdict.
